instructions:
Primary target: native macOS (Apple M5, 10 cores), release builds, the Aspire `Performance` category against the official .NET client in the same run (the harness's own measurement; `DXN_SIGNALR_PERF_SCALE=full`, three alternating rounds, median).

Acceptance gates per experiment:
1. The touched code's focused unit tests (`cargo test <filter>`, with and without `--features messagepack` where the code is protocol-specific), `cargo fmt --all --check`, and `cargo clippy --all-targets --test e2e --all-features -- -D warnings` pass. Stream/invoke/send behavior changes also run the matching native Aspire end-to-end scenario(s).
2. A full-scale all-workload Aspire Performance run (about 3 minutes): the targeted Rust metric improves by at least 3% over the current best, its Rust/.NET ratio improves, and no other Rust metric regresses beyond its observed round-to-round noise. A targeted metric whose rounds overlap the previous best is re-measured (targeted workload only) before deciding.
3. Profiler evidence (macOS `sample` on the perf process during the Aspire run) or Criterion (`hot_paths`, saved baseline `loop0`) shows the claimed mechanism.

Never change the perf harness, the .NET reference or the test service to move the numbers; the library is what is optimized. Public API and behavior stay unchanged.

Guard metrics (from experiment 30): benchmarks a change must not slow down are judged with ABBA-ordered interleaved runs (at least 2 pairs). A guard regresses only when the change's mean is worse than the control's by more than the declared bar AND every change round is worse than every control round. Targeted metrics keep their predeclared improvement thresholds on the mean.

atomicDiscipline.rule: Run exactly the printed hypothesis. If the attempted change fails, degrades, or suggests a different fix, revert to the checkpoint and finish this experiment as failure. Start a new experiment for the next idea.
